page: Amazon Web Services m3.large is a general purpose instance running on the Xen hypervisor, driven by an Intel Xeon E5-2670 v2 processor operating at 2.5 GHz. The server configuration provides 2 vCPUs derived from a single physical core with hyperthreading enabled, alongside 8.0 GB of system memory. Bundled local storage includes a 32 GB solid-state drive, accompanied by a 1 Gbps baseline network bandwidth. Accelerated computing capabilities are absent, as the instance features zero GPUs.

Hardware benchmark results reflect the older Ivy Bridge microarchitecture of the host platform. Compute throughput registers at the low end of modern profiles, with a single-core Geekbench score of 693.0, a multi-core Geekbench score of 802.0, and a PassMark CPU score of 1880.57. Memory bandwidth performance reaches 14.03 GB/sec on uncached large-block reads and 12.02 GB/sec on writes. In-memory data store workloads yield approximately 0.8 million Redis SET operations per second, while static web throughput reaches 1.95 GB/sec.

Because of its legacy resource density and lower compute efficiency compared to newer instance families, the m3.large presents diminished cost-performance value for compute-heavy applications. However, the inclusion of direct-attached local SSD storage offers predictable scratch space without provisioning external storage. The instance remains suitable for legacy testing environments, low-traffic web serving, basic background task processing, and small operational utilities that require a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio.
description: Amazon Web Services m3.large is a legacy general purpose instance powered by a 2.5 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2670 v2 processor on the x86_64 architecture. Managed via the Xen hypervisor, it provides 2 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 1 physical hyperthreaded core, 8.0 GB of RAM, and 1 Gbps baseline networking. Storage is bundled directly via a 32 GB local SSD, while GPU hardware is omitted. Benchmark results reflect entry-tier performance by modern standards, producing a multi-core Geekbench score of 802.0 and PassMark score of 1880.57. Memory bandwidth delivers 14.03 GB/sec for large un-cached reads, and Redis operations execute at 0.8 million SETs per second. Due to its older hardware baseline, the instance delivers low throughput per resource unit compared to modern families, positioning it primarily for legacy software validation, dev-test environments, lightweight background tasks, and low-volume web serving.
